summary: Updates RFC 6040 to clarify that its ECN propagation rules also cover IP tunnels where two IP headers are separated by a shim header. It surveys widely used tunnelling protocols with shims and updates several related RFCs.

plainLanguage.summary:
A tunnel wraps one IP packet inside another. When the network inside the tunnel is congested, routers mark packets so that the sender slows down. For that marking to survive the tunnel, the tunnel has to carry it from the inner header to the outer one.

RFC 9601 says that the rules written for this in RFC 6040 also cover tunnels that put other headers, such as GRE or L2TP, between the two IP headers. It also says how an operator must configure a tunnel that does not support this, so that a marking is not silently lost.

questions: how does ecn work in gre tunnels
subtitle: Clarifies that ECN propagation rules cover tunnels with shim headers, and tells operators how to make older tunnel ingresses safe.

tldr.problem: RFC 6040 defined how Explicit Congestion Notification passes through IP-in-IP tunnels, but its scope was ambiguous about tunnels with shim headers such as GRE or L2TP between the two IP headers, and it said nothing about tunnel ingresses that do not support ECN.
tldr.mechanism: It adds scoping text to RFC 6040, requires operators to configure a non-ECN tunnel ingress to zero the outer ECN field, sets rules for fragments, and gives update text for L2TP, GRE, Teredo and AMT.
tldr.outcome: ECN markings from a congested tunnel can propagate safely, and ingresses that cannot do so clear the outer ECN field to 0b00 instead of risking broken congestion feedback loops.

today: RFC 9601 was published in August 2024 and is a Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 6040, RFC 2661, RFC 2784, RFC 3931, RFC 4380 and RFC 7450, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: What the RFC Clarifies
sections.content:
RFC 6040 made the rules for propagating Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) consistent for all forms of IP-in-IP tunnel. ECN, defined in RFC 3168, is the two-bit field in the IP header that lets a router mark a packet as having crossed a congested link so that the sender reduces its rate.

A common pattern for tunnelling protocols is to encapsulate an inner IP header with one or more shim headers and then an outer IP header. Some shim headers are generic encapsulations and do not directly encapsulate an inner IP header; they can encapsulate link-layer headers, which in turn often encapsulate IP. The RFC uses the abbreviation IP-shim-(L2)-IP for tunnels of this shape.

This specification clarifies that the scope of RFC 6040 includes any IP-in-IP tunnel, including those with one or more shim headers and other encapsulations between the IP headers. Where necessary it updates the specifications of the relevant encapsulation protocols with the text needed to comply with RFC 6040. It also updates RFC 6040 to say how operators should configure a legacy tunnel ingress so that the system is not left in an unsafe state.
sections.plainLanguage: ECN is a pair of bits in the IP header that say a packet crossed a congested link. When a packet goes through a tunnel, that marking has to be copied into the outer header or the sender never learns the tunnel was congested. This RFC says the rules for that copying also apply when there are other headers between the two IP headers.

sections.title: The Scope of RFC 6040
sections.content:
The scoping statement in Section 1.1 of RFC 6040 had two problems. The first was ambiguity: it was intended to cover cases where shim headers sit between the IP headers, and many implementers read it that way, but the wording did not say so. This RFC adds text saying that it applies where an outer IP header encapsulates an inner IP header either directly or indirectly, by encapsulating other headers that in turn encapsulate, or might encapsulate, an inner IP header.

The second problem is that RFC 6040 is written as a specification that implementations may choose to claim compliance with, so it does not cover the case where an implementation cannot reach the inner IP header when adding or removing an outer header, or chooses not to propagate ECN. But the ECN field is not optional in an IP header, so any implementation that creates an outer header has to give the field some value, and the only safe value for an ingress that does not know whether the egress supports propagation is 0b00.

The RFC then explains when propagation is feasible. Where a shim and the outer header are added or removed in the same operation, the shim is a tightly coupled shim header, and it is often feasible to propagate the field. Where a tightly coupled shim sits over a header that encapsulates IP, digging into the encapsulation to find an inner IP header is a layering violation and cannot be required, though some implementations already look inside a Layer 2 header to map the Diffserv codepoint.

Propagation has to stay optional, for three reasons: legacy tunnels without ECN support already exist; a network may be designed so that there is no bottleneck inside the tunnel; and searching a Layer 2 header for an IP header may not be worth the performance cost.
sections.plainLanguage: The wording of RFC 6040 was ambiguous about shim headers, so this RFC adds explicit text. It also notes that an old tunnel endpoint that cannot propagate the marking must at least set the outer field to zero, and that digging inside a link-layer header to find the inner IP header is a layering violation that cannot be required.

sections.title: Making a Non-ECN Tunnel Ingress Safe by Configuration
sections.content:
Even where no attempt has been made to implement ECN propagation, an operator should be able to make a tunnel ingress safe by configuration. The main concern is that the ingress must clear the ECN capability in the outer IP header to zero if the tunnel egress does not implement the ECN logic that carries markings into the packet forwarded beyond the tunnel. Otherwise the non-ECN egress could discard a marking made inside the tunnel, which breaks the control loops that regulate the load over the tunnel.

The text added to Section 4.3 of RFC 6040 says that, whether or not an implementation claims compliance with RFC 6040, RFC 4301 or RFC 3168, the ingress MUST be configured to zero the outer ECN field when the egress is known not to support propagation, when the behaviour of the egress is not known or might be paired with the ingress dynamically, or when an IP header might be encapsulated inside a non-IP header that the ingress is encapsulating but does not inspect. The ingress MUST NOT alter the ECN field of the arriving IP header that will become the inner header.

Two implementation requirements follow so that the operator can comply. The ingress MUST NOT treat the former Type of Service octet of IPv4 or the former Traffic Class octet of IPv6 as a single 8-bit field, because that would link the ECN and Diffserv propagation in a way that is inconsistent with the 6-bit Diffserv field. And it SHOULD be able to be configured to zero the ECN field of the outer header.
sections.plainLanguage: An old tunnel endpoint that cannot carry the congestion marking into the outer header must at least set that field to zero. Otherwise the far end may drop a marking that was made inside the tunnel, and the sender never slows down. The rule covers the case where the operator cannot even be sure what the far end does.

sections.title: Fragmentation and Reassembly
sections.content:
RFC 6040 said nothing about the ECN field during fragmentation or reassembly, and this RFC fills that gap. If a tunnel ingress fragments a packet, it MUST set the outer ECN field of all the fragments to the same value it would have used if it had not fragmented the packet.

At a tunnel egress, two rules apply when reassembling outer fragments into one packet. The packet MUST be discarded if the ECN fields of the outer headers being reassembled consist of a mixture of Not ECN-Capable Transport and other ECN codepoints. And if there is a mix of ECT(0) and ECT(1) outer fragments, the reassembled packet MUST be set to ECT(1).

The RFC gives the reason for the second rule. RFC 3168 originally treated ECT(0) and ECT(1) as equivalent, but it has since been updated by RFC 8311 to make ECT(1) available for congestion marking differences. The rule does not depend on the current experimental use of ECT(1) for Low Latency, Low Loss, and Scalable throughput, and it is compatible with Pre-Congestion Notification, which uses two levels of congestion severity ranked from highest to lowest as Congestion Experienced, ECT(1), ECT(0).
sections.plainLanguage: When a tunnel splits a packet into fragments, all the fragments must carry the same outer congestion value. When the far end puts them back together, a mix of the two transport-capable values becomes the more severe one, and a mix with the not-capable value makes the packet get thrown away.

sections.title: Tunnels with Tightly Coupled Shims
sections.content:
The RFC lists the encapsulations with tightly coupled shim headers, in rough chronological order, limited to Standards Track or widely deployed protocols. It notes that the updated scope of RFC 6040 is not limited to this list. The list covers PPTP, L2TPv2 and L2TPv3 and its derivatives, GRE and NVGRE, GTP, Teredo, CAPWAP, LISP, AMT, VXLAN and VXLAN-GPE, the Network Service Header, Geneve, direct tunnelling of an IP packet in a UDP/IP datagram, and TCP encapsulation of IKE and IPsec packets.

Several of these already do the right thing. CAPWAP already specifies ECN propagation and capability negotiation, and interworks with the RFC 6040 updates to RFC 3168 without change. LISP made the ECN propagation procedures of RFC 3168 mandatory from the start, and the changes are backwards compatible, so LISP endpoints do not need to negotiate their capabilities. Section 3.1.11 of RFC 8085 already says that a tunnel carrying an IP header inside a UDP/IP datagram must follow RFC 6040, and this RFC's clarification extends that to cases with a shim header as well as a UDP header. The Geneve specification already refers to RFC 6040.

Where a protocol is under IETF change control, update text is given. For protocols outside IETF control, implementations are RECOMMENDED to comply with RFC 6040, and their specifications are RECOMMENDED to be updated to require it. PPTP needs no update, because L2TP was developed as a standardised replacement.
sections.plainLanguage: Many tunnel protocols put a header between the two IP headers: GRE, L2TP, GTP, Teredo, AMT and others. This RFC lists them and says which already behave correctly. For the rest it either supplies the wording to add or recommends that their specifications require RFC 6040.

sections.title: Negotiating ECN Support in L2TP and AMT
sections.content:
For L2TPv2 and L2TPv3, where the outer PSN header and the payload inside the Layer 2 header are both IP, the L2TP Control Connection Endpoint propagates the ECN field at ingress and egress by following the rules of Section 4 of RFC 6040. Before encapsulating data packets, an ingress must check that the egress supports ECN propagation. If it does, the ingress can use the normal mode, copying the ECN field from inner to outer. Otherwise the ingress must use the compatibility mode and clear the outer IP ECN field to 0b00.

The support can be determined statically by configuration, or dynamically during the setup of each control connection using the new ECN Capability AVP, whose attribute type is 103 and whose length before hiding is 6 octets. It may appear in the Start-Control-Connection-Request and Start-Control-Connection-Reply messages, may be hidden, and is optional. The Vendor ID is the IETF Vendor ID of 0.

When an endpoint sends the AVP it says that it supports propagation; when the AVP is absent the sender does not support it. If the initiator supports ECN it sends the AVP in the request. If the tunnel terminator supports ECN it returns the AVP in the reply, and both ends can then use the normal mode. If the terminator does not support ECN it ignores the AVP and replies without it, and the initiator treats the absence as a sign that the terminator cannot do it, so it uses the compatibility mode.

AMT, which is a tightly coupled shim header inside a UDP/IP datagram, follows the same pattern with a different mechanism. Bit 14 of the AMT Request Message, counting from 0, is defined as the AMT Gateway ECN Capability flag. When it is set, the sender supports RFC 6040 propagation; when it is clear, it does not. A relay that supports propagation stores the capability with the gateway's address and then copies the ECN field from inner to outer when it tunnels datagrams to that gateway. A relay that does not support propagation ignores the flag, and its operator is still expected to configure it to comply with the safety rules.
sections.plainLanguage: L2TP and AMT tunnels are set up automatically, so the two ends need to tell each other whether they can carry the congestion marking. L2TP does this with a new option in its setup messages, and AMT with a single flag bit. If the far end says no, the near end sets the outer field to zero instead of copying it across.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that the security considerations of RFC 6040 and RFC 9599 apply equally to the scope it defines.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC adds nothing new here. The existing guidance on ECN in tunnels, and the general guidance on propagating ECN into other protocols, both apply.

viz.caption: WHEN PROPAGATING ECN ACROSS A SHIM IS FEASIBLE

items.title: Shim and outer header together
items.text: When they are added or removed in the same operation, propagation is usually feasible.

items.title: Shim over an encapsulating header
items.text: Finding an IP header inside a Layer 2 header is a layering violation and cannot be required.

items.title: Legacy tunnels
items.text: Tunnels with no ECN support already exist, so propagation must stay optional.

items.title: Performance
items.text: Searching inside a Layer 2 header may not be worth the cost.

cells: The tunnel egress is known to support ECN propagation
The egress behaviour is unknown, or known not to support propagation

fields.desc: Bit 14 counting from 0 is the AMT Gateway ECN Capability flag; when set, the sender supports ECN propagation.

fields.desc: Other bits stay reserved, sent as zero and ignored on receipt.
